report:
**Conclusion: no—reliable evidence does not show that ivermectin lowers the risk of death from COVID-19.**

Early reports of reduced mortality were based largely on small trials with few deaths and important methodological problems. The WHO’s evidence review judged evidence for mortality (as well as ventilation and admission) to be **very low certainty**, because trials were small and had design limitations.

Subsequent, better-designed and larger placebo-controlled randomized trials did not find a meaningful clinical benefit. The TOGETHER trial tested ivermectin in high-risk symptomatic outpatients and found no clinical benefit; the US ACTIV-6 trial also found no benefit even using a higher dose for six days. A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 33 randomized trials (10,489 participants) likewise reported no reduction in mortality.

This does not mean ivermectin is never useful: it is an established treatment for certain parasitic infections. But it should not be used to treat or prevent COVID-19 outside a clinical trial, and veterinary formulations or excessive doses can be dangerous. For an individual case, proven COVID treatments depend on timing, illness severity, drug interactions, and risk factors—consult a clinician promptly.
